texte.35eb98e023e4: F1: Why does Black leave the bishop on b4? The answer: the pawn on e3 is much more dangerous than the bishop, because after {z1} comes {z2}. White has only two replies: {z3} loses the queen after {z4}, because the d-file is open, so {z5}, and now comes the point: {z6} Black promotes to a knight, which is an underpromotion (Chapter 0). Only the knight gives check here. With a promotion to a queen, on the other hand, White could first trade queens with {z7} and then capture the new queen on g1. After {z8}, {z9} wins the queen, since the king on e2 and the queen on d1 stand on the same diagonal. If White plays {z10} instead, after {z11} the king stands defenseless out in the open. The warning sign was W2: the white queen on d1 stands on the same file as the black queen on d8, with only White's own bishop on d2 in between, so the d-file is open as soon as the bishop moves to b4. The right move is {z12}. Even better, White avoids {z13} in the first place and plays {z14}. The trap-setter test: {z15} is a good move even if White does not fall for it. Remember: if an enemy piece stands undefended, ready to be taken, first look for the check your opponent has afterwards.
texte.ff9ab286e120: After 6. Bxb4?? exf2+ 7. Ke2 comes 7... fxg1=N+!: the underpromotion gives check, and White then loses the queen, or the white king stands defenseless out in the open. The right move is 6. fxe3; the warning sign was the open d-file between the queens as soon as the bishop on d2 moves away.
texte.e86f03dfbfd1: Black has moved the knight away from c6 with {z1}, and suddenly the pawn on e5 stands undefended. Go through the full trap check: Which warning sign do you see? What happens two replies ahead after {z2}? What do you play instead? And does {z3} pass the trap-setter test?
texte.b214d6ee2c97: The warning sign is W5: the pawn on e5 seems to be free for the taking. F1: Why does Black move the only defender of e5 away? F2: After {z1}, {z2} attacks the bishop on b5. If it retreats with {z3} or {z4}, {z5} follows: the queen gives check and at the same time attacks the knight on e5 along the fifth rank, a double attack as in the Blackburne Shilling Gambit. After {z6}, Black has won a piece. If White instead saves the knight with {z7}, it threatens {z8} itself. {z9} would therefore be a blunder. With {z10}, Black takes the d6 square away from the knight, the bishop on b5 remains attacked, and Black wins a piece for two pawns. The right course for White is to leave the pawn alone and develop, for example with {z11} or {z12}. The trap-setter test is not as clear-cut as for most traps in this chapter: {z13} is playable, and the knight wants to come into play via g6. But it moves a second time and delays development. So this trap is only partly recommendable as a weapon of your own. Remember: if the only defender of a pawn moves away voluntarily, the pawn is rarely really free.
texte.34ec4fd0c8e2: After 5. Nxe5? c6! the bishop has to retreat, and 6... Qa5+ attacks the king and the knight on e5 at the same time. White leaves the pawn alone and develops with 5. Nc3 or 5. O-O; if the only defender moves away voluntarily, the pawn is rarely really free.
texte.1f430cbb6328: Match each of the five warning signs W1 to W5 from Section 4.2 with at least one trap from this chapter. For each one, name the piece or the line where you can see the sign on the board.
texte.8fccb349d1bc: W1 undefended piece: the rook on a8 in the clamp trap, the pawn on g2 and the knight on e5 in the Blackburne Shilling Gambit, the queen on h3 in the queen trap in the Danish Gambit. W2 dangerous line: the g5–d8 diagonal in the Elephant Trap, the e-file between the queen on e7 and the king on e1 in the Kieninger Trap. W3 king without air: the white king on e1 in the Kieninger Trap and in the Blackburne Shilling Gambit, the black king after {z1} in the Légal Trap, and the black king on e8 in the Benko Trap. W4 double duty: the knight on f3 in the Siberian Trap, which is the only piece effectively defending h2. W5 gift: the white queen on d1 in the Légal Trap, the white queen on f3 in the Halosar Trap, the pawn on d5 in the Elephant Trap, the pawn on d4 in Noah's Ark Trap, the pawn on e5 in the Blackburne Shilling Gambit and in the King's Gambit Declined. Remember: a warning sign does not tell you what is threatened, but it shows you where you need to calculate.
texte.252bff9e6788: Every warning sign shows up on a piece or a line, for example the undefended queen on h3 in the Danish Gambit (W1), the open e-file in the Kieninger Trap (W2), or the queen on d1 as a gift in the Légal Trap (W5). A sign does not tell you what is threatened, but where you need to calculate.
texte.10593be11c12: In the Légal Trap, White has just played {z1} ({v1}). You are Black and have realized that {z2} loses. How do you win back the knight on e5, and what does it cost you? Use F2 to calculate two replies ahead.
texte.42872dc8b4a0: The solid alternative is to win back the knight on e5 at once, for example with {z1}: the black pawn on d6 captures on e5 and so takes back the white knight. This is not entirely free, though: the knight on f3 is gone, the pin no longer exists, and the bishop on h5 now stands undefended. So after {z2}, White is a pawn up. After {z3}, too, White keeps an extra pawn. Being a pawn down is unpleasant, but far better than being mated. Remember: once you have spotted a trap, look for the move that costs you the least.
texte.5e444c4ce5d9: Instead of 6... Bxd1??, Black wins the knight back at once, for example with 6... dxe5. Because the pin is gone, White takes the undefended bishop with 7. Qxh5 and is a pawn up: annoying, but much better than being mated.
